newsitem.title: USA: Olympic bomb suspect may be cleared soon - lawyer.
newsitem.headline: Olympic bomb suspect may be cleared soon - lawyer.

text.p: Federal investigators have dropped their surveillance of Olympic bomb suspect Richard Jewell and have agreed to clear him of suspicion if they are satisifed with his answers to a weekend interrogation, one of his attorneys said on Tuesday.

Lin Wood, a civil lawyer with the former security guard's four-member legal team, also said the FBI on Tuesday returned the last of the property confiscated during a search of his suburban Atlanta apartment, namely several rifles and handguns.

Jewell, 33, so far the only named suspect in the investigation, spent nearly six hours on Sunday answering questions from the FBI about his behaviour during the July 27 pipebomb attack, which left two people dead and more than 100 injured at Centennial Olympic Park in downtown Atlanta.
His lawyer said the interview was part of a deal with U.S. Attorney Kent Alexander that could soon lead to Jewell's exoneration.

"In return for allowing him to be interviewed, they committed to us in good faith to expedite their consideration of his interview, and if they are satisfied with his interview, the U.S. attorney will issue a written letter indicating that he is no longer a subject or target of the investigation," said Wood.
"We hope that letter will include some statement that the Department of Justice regrets the problems, inconvenience and harships that it's caused on Richard and his mother," he added.

"We expect to get that letter because we believe that Richard's told them everything they need to know or want to know, and he's telling the truth he didn't do this. And hopefully they'll reach that conclusion in the next few days or the next two or three weeks."
G. Watson Bryant, Jewell's lead attorney, later said federal officials have promised to reach a decision on Jewell within three weeks.
"They said that they 'hope to get to you' within three weeks," he said.

"They could give us a letter today, but I doubt it. They've got to take a five-and-a-half-hour interview and they've got to go through it and make sure they're comfortable saying he's no longer a subject or target and that they regret what happened to him."
A spokesman for the U.S. Attorney's Office in Atlanta declined to comment on the case.
Wood is one of two civil lawyers hired by Jewell to help him determine whether there are grounds for a lawsuit against both the U.S. government and members of the news media.
On the night of the explosion, Jewell worked as a security guard at a nearby Olympic pavillion operated by AT&T Corp for the Atlanta Summer Games.
At first, he was hailed as a hero for finding the green knapsack that carried the crude pipebomb. But he was named as a suspect a few days later and has since been forced into seclusion.
The FBI seached the apartment he shares with mother, a tool shed in northern Georgia and a rural cabin where he once lived, confiscating property at each site.

Jewell, who has never been charged in any crime and steadfastly maintains his innocence, has said through his attorneys that FBI leaks to the news media about his role as a suspect have ruined his chances of finding gainful employment.

Until last week, FBI agents kept him under round-the-clock surveillance. Then overt surveillance was replaced by what his attorneys described as covert surveillance. Now, Wood says there appears to be no surveillance at all.
"I don't think there's any surveillance on Richard Jewell now. At least since last Thursday, there has been no surveillance," said Wood.
"On Saturday, all of his property and his mother's property was returned, with the exception of his guns...this morning they returned his guns to him."
